subject: wright-brothers
title: The Wright Way: Engineering by Experiment
summary: Control, bad data, and a propeller that is really a spinning wing.

keys.prompt: What did the Wrights treat as the key problem of flight, and how did they solve it?
keys.answer: Control. They twisted the wing tips in opposite directions (wing warping) so one side lifted more and the plane banked.

keys.prompt: When published lift data didn't match their gliders, what did the Wrights do?
keys.answer: Built their own wind tunnel and measured lift and drag on model wings instead of trusting the numbers.

keys.prompt: Flying into a headwind, how do airspeed and groundspeed relate?
keys.answer: Airspeed is about groundspeed plus the headwind: on Dec 17, 1903, 6.8 + 27 ≈ 34 mph.

cards.title: The underdogs
cards.text: Samuel Langley had government money and the newspapers watching. Two bicycle makers from Ohio worked in near obscurity. The bike makers flew first. How?

cards.question: Langley had government money and the newspapers watching. What do you think was the problem the Wrights solved first?

options.text: Control: steering and balancing the plane
Making the plane lighter than air

cards.reveal: Control. Lilienthal steered by shifting his body weight. The Wrights twisted the wing tips ("wing warping") so one side lifted more and the plane banked.

cards.title: Control was the real problem
cards.text: Glider pioneer Otto Lilienthal steered by shifting his body weight. The Wrights twisted the wing tips in opposite directions ("wing warping"). One side then made more lift than the other, which banked the plane.
cards.example: They tested the idea on a kite with a five-foot wingspan in 1899 before risking a person.

cards.title: When the data is wrong
cards.text: Their 1900 and 1901 gliders made much less lift than published data predicted. Instead of guessing, they built a wind tunnel in fall 1901 with instruments to measure lift and drag on small model wings.
cards.example: Their 1902 glider, built from their own data, made 700 to 1,000 flights. The best went 622.5 feet in 26 seconds.

examples_by_interest.golf: Say a golf magazine claims a new driver adds 10 yards. The Wright move: test it yourself with the same balls and many swings, and write down the real distances.
examples_by_interest.soccer: Say a training video promises a new kicking style adds power. The Wright move: film 20 kicks each way and measure, instead of trusting the video.
examples_by_interest.business: Say a report says the market for your product is huge. The Wright move: run a small test sale and measure real demand before betting big.

cards.title: A propeller is a spinning wing
cards.text: Boat propeller theory did not help much. The Wrights treated a propeller as a wing turned on its side and spun, making "lift" that pushes forward. The 1903 Flyer had two propellers turning in opposite directions to cancel a twisting force.
cards.example: They built their own 12-horsepower engine with their bicycle shop mechanic, Charles Taylor.

why.q: Why treat a propeller as a spinning wing?
why.a: A wing makes lift from air flowing over it. Turn a wing on its side and spin it, and that "lift" pushes the plane forward.

cards.title: Do the math
cards.text: On December 17, 1903, the wind was 27 mph. Orville's groundspeed was only 6.8 mph, so his airspeed was about 34 mph. Lift depends on air moving over the wings, so a headwind helps you get airborne.
cards.example: Flight 1: 120 feet in 12 seconds. Flight 4, with Wilbur: 852 feet in 59 seconds.

cards.prompt: In "Gutenberg's Startup: Combining Old Tech" the breakthrough was a system, not one part. What was the Wrights' system?
cards.model: Control (wing warping), their own lift data (the wind tunnel), and efficient propellers with a light engine, all made to work together.

cards.question: Langley relied on raw power. The Wrights relied on control and skill. In golf, soccer, or a business you'd start, what is the "control problem" people overlook?
nudges: Is distance or accuracy the bigger problem for most golfers?
What would your version of a wind tunnel be: a cheap test before the big bet?

questions.q: Into a 27-mph headwind, Orville's groundspeed was 6.8 mph. About what was his airspeed?

options.why: Yes: 27 + 6.8 is about 34. The air moved over the wings at about 34 mph.
That subtracts the numbers. Into a headwind, airspeed is groundspeed plus wind speed.
That is speed over the sand. The wings "feel" the air, which was moving toward them too.

options.text: Twisting the wing tips so one side lifts more and the plane banks
options.why: Right. It steers with air forces instead of body weight.
That was Lilienthal's method. The Wrights wanted something that worked on bigger aircraft.

options.text: Flapping the wings like a bird
options.why: The wings did not flap. They twisted slightly at the tips.

questions.q: Why did the Wrights build a wind tunnel?

options.text: Their gliders made less lift than the published data predicted.
options.why: Exactly. They tested the numbers instead of trusting them.
The tunnel measured lift and drag on model wings.
They worked mostly out of the public eye. The tunnel was for data.
